content.text: An Error Boundary catches errors thrown while React renders the components below it, and shows a fallback instead of a blank screen. It doesn't see errors from event handlers, timers or ordinary promise callbacks, because those run outside rendering. Catch those yourself, or in React 19, run the work in a transition so its error reaches the boundary.
The checkout page is wrapped in an

with a friendly "Something went wrong, try again" fallback, and the team considers it crash-proof. Then the payment API starts rejecting some requests. Customers click "Pay", the button switches to "Paying…" and stays there forever. No fallback, no message, no retry. The only trace is an "Uncaught (in promise)" line in the console that nobody is watching. The boundary works fine; the error simply never went through it.
around everything inside it. Any error thrown anywhere in its subtree, whether in rendering, a click handler or a fetch callback, ends up in the fallback.

It's easy to believe because the JSX looks that way: the boundary visibly wraps the button, so surely it wraps what the button does. Testing usually confirms it, since the quickest way to try a boundary is a component that throws during render, and that case works perfectly. And the word "boundary" suggests a fence around a region of the app, not around one particular phase of React's work.
A boundary catches errors from rendering

React's docs describe the job precisely: if a component throws during rendering, React removes the UI by default, and a boundary lets you show fallback UI for the part that crashed instead. A boundary is a class component with
, which switches it into an error state, and usually
, which gets the error plus a
for logging. It works because React itself is calling your components. When one throws, React is right there, finds the nearest boundary above it, and renders the fallback in its place.
Handlers and async code run outside rendering
The docs list what boundaries don't catch: event handlers, asynchronous code such as

callbacks, server-side rendering, and errors thrown in the boundary itself rather than its children. By the time a click handler runs, rendering has already finished and the screen is in a valid state. A
callback or the code after an

runs even later, on its own. When that code throws, there's no render in progress for React to abandon, so the error goes to the browser instead: an uncaught exception, or for an async function, a rejected promise that nothing handles.

Not every failure deserves a fallback, though. A declined card is something the user can fix, and replacing the whole checkout is a harsh way to say so. For expected failures, catch the error in the handler with
and show an inline message next to the button. Keep the boundary for what you didn't expect.

Keep fallbacks simple, and add a top-level boundary

content.text: If the boundary or its fallback throws, the error goes to the next boundary up. If there's none, React removes the UI it was rendering. Keep fallback components tiny and data-free, and put one boundary near the root as a last line of defense. Note too that the standalone
imported from React isn't tied to a component, so a boundary can't handle errors from its transitions.
